item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I really liked this one. I liked the charm of the escalation of procedures for the specimens, without resorting to exotic things like explosive failsafe. Just increasing the caution and number of guards. I think it was clever to say that only 1 guard is needed for -1 because it poses a minimal threat.

The description part was when I went, "this is boring, I don't like it."

Then the specimen list brought back the charm of the procedure part. I disagree with the above suggestion about putting in some expunged log. I think this has found the sweet spot of how much to tell. It tells what is on the crabs, and gives you a sense of the increading sizes of the crabs nicely.

In short, I like how it takes a very simple idea and actually tells enough to let me imagine the horror, without needing over the top things like decimated expeditions or dramatic expungements.

item.content:encoded:
First, crabs do not have hands. Call them pincers, grabbing limbs or upper appendages, but right now it looks like the log was written by a middle school kid instead of a scientist. Legs seem hardly professional too, even if used more commonly regarding arthropods' walking appendages.

From the article…

Specimens of SCP-863 are born without limbs, and undergo a process in which they utilize the limbs of other organisms, or even whole organisms in lieu of their own.

In that log, the hand was from a human. Same with the reference to legs, or at least some of them.

Furthermore, calling the legs of a crab "legs" is fine. The technical term would be "peropods" though. Clinical tone isn't about using fancy words: it's stating things clearly without the use of slang.

And, speaking of which, why does every described specimen adds to itself only six walking appendages instead of eight

Because the japanese spider crab only has six legs, which this SCP is stated to resemble.

item.content:encoded:
First, crabs do not have hands. Call them pincers, grabbing limbs or upper appendages, but right now it looks like the log was written by a middle school kid instead of a scientist. Legs seem hardly professional too, even if used more commonly regarding arthropods' walking appendages. It's a minor change and I'd correct it, but I'm not sure if I'm allowed to. And, speaking of which, why does every described specimen adds to itself only six walking appendages instead of eight?

Also, there seems to be something off between the last part of procedures and beginning of description. Every wild one must be killed… But it's a common species in the area it inhabits? It's hardly possible, would take WAY more funds than O5s would like to spend on some limb-stealing crabs and can destabilize the ecosystem they're a part of. Maybe extermination applying only to individuals reaching a legspan of [REDACTED] instead, just to keep ones being dangerous to humans down?

Not a fan, to be honest. No vote.
